tips: Start with the user’s goal before choosing features or technology.
Make the next useful action easy to find.
Organize navigation around user tasks, not your company’s structure.
Use familiar patterns when they help people act with confidence.
Reveal advanced options when users need them.
Keep essential controls in predictable places.
Give each screen a clear purpose and visual hierarchy.
Use whitespace to clarify relationships between elements.
Write button labels that describe what will happen.
Pair unfamiliar icons with clear text labels.
Use plain language without stripping away necessary meaning.
Put important information where users need it to make a decision.
Make content easy to scan without assuming nobody reads.
Show the consequence of an action before users commit.
Keep help close to the task it supports.
Teach features through useful first actions.
Let people experience value before asking for unnecessary commitments.
Make empty states explain what belongs here and how to begin.
Offer sensible defaults that users can inspect and change.
Support shortcuts for experienced users without hiding basic controls.
Design accessibility into components before they spread across the product.
Make every essential task usable with a keyboard.
Keep keyboard focus visible and unobscured.
Give controls accessible names that match their visible labels.
Communicate meaning with more than color alone.
Maintain readable contrast for text and essential interface elements.
Support text resizing without clipping content or losing functionality.
Make touch targets generous and leave space between competing actions.
Respect reduced-motion preferences.
Provide alternatives to dragging, swiping, and other complex gestures.
Never make hover the only way to discover essential information.
Announce important status changes without overwhelming screen-reader users.
Provide captions for video and transcripts for audio.
Make authentication compatible with password managers and pasted credentials.
Test layouts with long translations and right-to-left languages.
Ask only for information needed to complete the task.
Keep form labels visible after users start typing.
Explain formatting requirements before input fails.
Preserve entered information when validation finds a problem.
Describe errors clearly and offer a specific recovery action.
Confirm successful actions with feedback proportional to their importance.
Distinguish between saving, saved, and failed-to-save states.
Preserve work through interruptions, timeouts, and connection failures.
Provide undo when an action can reasonably be reversed.
Reserve confirmation dialogs for consequences that warrant interruption.
Show honest progress instead of invented percentages.
Keep layouts stable as content loads.
Make search forgiving of typos and variations in terminology.
Explain active filters and make them easy to clear.
Help users recover from zero search results.
Make notification frequency and delivery channels easy to control.
Show prices, limits, and renewal terms before commitment.
Make cancellation and account deletion easy to find and understand.
Request permissions when their purpose becomes clear.
Give people meaningful control over collected data and personalization.
Add AI where it improves a user outcome you can evaluate.
Choose chat, forms, or direct controls based on the task.
Show useful examples so users do not need to master prompting.
Make AI capabilities discoverable through concrete tasks.
Explain relevant AI limitations where they affect user decisions.
Identify AI-generated content when its origin matters.
Separate generated suggestions from actions already completed.
Let users edit AI output directly.
Support targeted revisions without forcing users to regenerate everything.
Preserve previous versions so users can compare and recover.
Make AI summaries link back to the underlying material.
Keep exceptions and caveats visible when summarizing.
Provide inspectable sources for claims that require verification.
Distinguish retrieved evidence from generated interpretation.
Show uncertainty in terms users can act on.
Display confidence scores only when they are calibrated and understandable.
Let AI acknowledge missing information instead of inventing an answer.
Ask clarifying questions when ambiguity would materially change the result.
Make consequential assumptions visible and easy to correct.
Let users control which files, messages, or records inform an AI response.
Explain which connected accounts an AI feature can access.
Separate permission to read information from permission to change it.
Make an AI agent’s authorized scope clear before it acts.
Match approval requirements to an action’s consequences and reversibility.
Ask users to approve a concrete preview of consequential changes.
Keep authorized routine work moving without repeated permission prompts.
Provide accessible controls to pause or stop an AI task.
Explain what stopping a task cancels and what has already happened.
Show whether an agent is working, waiting, blocked, or finished.
Report partial completion and failures explicitly.
Keep an inspectable history of actions an agent performed.
Let users set time, spending, or usage limits for autonomous work.
Make AI memory visible, editable, and deletable.
Distinguish temporary task context from information remembered across sessions.
Make microphone, camera, and screen-sharing activity unmistakable.
Provide text alternatives to voice interactions.
Let users correct speech recognition before consequential actions occur.
Offer a useful fallback when AI is unavailable or cannot finish.
Preserve context when handing an AI interaction to human support.
Test AI experiences with ambiguous requests, incorrect outputs, and interrupted tasks.
Evaluate AI quality across languages, abilities, and relevant user groups.
Include the effort of checking and correcting AI output in usability measures.
Use AI to support research analysis while keeping findings traceable to participant evidence.
Treat synthetic users as hypotheses to explore, not evidence of real user behavior.
Reevaluate user journeys after AI updates; changed behavior can invalidate earlier design decisions.
